doc.title: Bill Dobbins interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rochester, New York, January 11, 2012

title: Nervous of silence, Ken Wilber and Arthur Koestler
summary: Inner life, noise everywhere, Wilber's book and Koestler's trilogy on creativity.

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: Life philosophy: faith, karma and how to live

blocks.x: Nervous of silence. That’s another phenomenon also I think more of our time too because we’re surrounded with so much extraneous noise all the time. Because every time you go into a restaurant or a shopping mall or anywhere, some kind of music or noise is ubiquitous. And because of that, even the very idea that there is, or could be, an inner life, which is my real life — I mean that’s where the action is all the time, whether I’m looking at you or looking out the window here, or listening to a piece of music, or having a conversation with my wife or whatever it is, even though it’s all happening out there, the experience and interpretation and mediation of that, if there is any, it all has to happen in here. One of the most profound books that I think I’ve read maybe in my life actually is a book by Ken Wilber, a really extraordinary American philosopher, called A Brief History of Everything. And two of the things that I found extraordinarily useful in this book — I think he wrote it around ’89, late 80s or early 90s — one is that the evolutionary process — and this is an idea also that was explored a little bit by Arthur Koestler, a really brilliant novelist and humanist and writer who was born in Budapest and grew up and was educated in England. He died I think in the late 60s or early 70s. But in one of his books — I can’t remember if it’s The Act of Creation or The Sleepwalkers. He wrote a trilogy of books — The Sleepwalkers, The Act of Creation, and The Ghost in the Machine. The Sleepwalkers is history of science in the time of the Greeks or before, up to Isaac Newton. And it’s called The Sleepwalkers because of the faulty nature in which these men came upon these different things and even the reluctance because of the censorship of the church and government agencies to even let out new realizations once they were made, because you could die for it. Like Oscar Wilde said if you tell people the truth you’d better be able to make them laugh or they will kill you. And the second book, The Act of Creation is, he makes a lot of interesting analogies between creativity in the arts and on the one hand, on the sublime end, the life of the mystic and the inner life, and on the other end the humor end, because creativity has to do with the ability to notice and make use of the intersections of two different planes of existence or two different ways of looking at the same thing. And in humor that’s where the joke comes from. But of course that same phenomenon happens in terms of — for lack of a better term — spiritual experience — our experience of the world that we can’t see, which is for you and I probably the most important stuff you know.
